Its symbolic core is written in Catala in a literate style that keeps statute and formalisation aligned and was developed through pair programming, with open-textured terms represented as boolean inputs where neural components couple to the symbolic solver. A neural routine structures a case's natural-language facts into boolean and date inputs. Neural subroutines resolve the open-textured terms through case-based reasoning over Dutch civil judgments, retrieved through a pipeline that filters on the requirement being resolved and expands along the procedural chain of a case. Segmenting and labelling those judgments attains high precision and recall against a manually annotated gold standard of 100 judgments. On ten hand-annotated cases the neuro-symbolic model handles most criteria reasonably but struggles with the knowledge requirement. Retrieval depth shows no clear quantitative effect, although retrieved judgments provide explicit grounding in prior case law.

title: Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning
summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens with bidirectional context. As these models reach real-world deployment, machine unlearning becomes essential. This process aims to remove the influence of a designated "forget set" without retraining from scratch, so that sensitive, copyrighted, or restricted content can no longer be elicited while preserving retained capabilities. Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU) is the first publicly available unlearning method customized for these models: it tunes the model $p_θ$ to match a frozen prompt-masked anchor $p_{\mathrm{anchor}}$ on the forget set by minimizing the anchor-last divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_θ\Vert p_{\mathrm{anchor}})$. We identify two failure modes of MDU. First, random answer masking can leave key forget tokens visible to the anchor even when the question is fully masked. Second, at a memorized (near-one-hot) prediction, the anchor-last logit gradient vanishes while the anchor-first divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{anchor}} \Vert p_θ)$ logit gradient does not. As a result, MDU training stalls on the tokens we most need to forget. Backed by theoretical and empirical analyses, we propose Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU): anchor-first KL divergence toward a frozen anchor whose entire answer span is masked. On TOFU and RWKU benchmarks using LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, our EMDU matches or exceeds the forgetting of MDU and adapted AR baselines, while better preserving retain utility.

title: World of SWECraft: Agent Collaboration at Scale via Simulated Software Worlds
summary: As teams of AI agents take on larger projects and long-standing open problems, agent collaboration offers another dimension for scaling inference-time compute. To understand what makes such collaboration effective and scalable, we develop Software World, a framework for simulating multi-agent coworking in realistic software ecosystems. It comes with a pipeline to create environments of real, interdependent Python packages of different topics, sizes, and dependency structures, which we call software worlds. In a simulation, agents maintain packages in the world with a high-level goal of improving software efficiency, and they are free to discover tasks to work on and collaborate with others. We evaluate agents' work in a world collectively by measuring speedup in hidden dependent packages. The framework allows us to study different elements of collaboration by varying communication, ownership, and resource allocation. We run simulations in three different worlds, totaling more than 10,000 hours of agent work across eight models. Overall, performance improvement scales with inference-time compute, with the best model improving downstream efficiency by up to 31%. We show that most agents can find meaningful tasks via collaboration, but some frontier models can prematurely stop looking for improvements and make little progress. We release the simulation framework and traces to support future studies of agent collaboration at https://szj.io/sw.

title: Beyond Static Leaderboards: Capability-Focused Evaluation with Structural Diversity for Time Series Foundation Models
summary: Static public benchmarks for time series foundation models (TSFMs) typically have fixed and narrow test distributions. Their repeated reuse encourages benchmark-specific tuning, making reported performance reflect adaptation to the fixed test set rather than genuine forecasting generalization. In addition, a single aggregate score cannot fully characterize model capabilities across distinct temporal structures and input relationships. We propose CaFE (Capability-Focused Evaluation), a refreshable evaluation extension grounded in original benchmark data that enriches static benchmarks with structural diversity and enriches single-score black-box evaluation with multi-dimensional, capability-oriented assessment. CaFE first profiles the original benchmark and defines eight Structural Features (SFs) that characterize its temporal structure. For each SF, it resamples the original data according to its structural support, removes edge-of-distribution samples, and augments the retained samples by varying the SF's salience, producing samples with different structural profiles. After filtering out out-of-distribution samples while preserving diversity, CaFE yields a refreshed evaluation set. TSFMs are then evaluated on this set using both conventional forecast-error metrics and intervention-response metrics, giving each model a per-feature capability profile alongside endpoint accuracy. Experiments on GIFT-Eval and FEV-Mini20 show that CaFE yields stable evaluation results and reveals per-feature strengths and weaknesses that a single aggregate score hides. Moreover, on genuine data filtered by structural condition, models selected by CaFE outperform those chosen by the aggregate leaderboard. CaFE therefore makes model selection conditional on the structural response of interest.

title: Semi-supervised learning on singular data sets
summary: We propose to model singular data clouds by subanalytic sets, and develop an approach to semi-supervised learning in this setting. It relies on a Morrey-type embedding for Sobolev spaces relative to globally subanalytic measures with possibly singular support. As an illustration, we present a greedy method based on a Monte Carlo approximation of the Sobolev norm of the candidate solutions. We report numerical experiments on point clouds sampled from real algebraic varieties, as well as a test on a classification problem based on MNIST images downsampled into $7\times7$.

title: Location, Location, Generation: Where You Ask Matters for Generative Engine Optimization
summary: Generative search engines answer local and commercial questions with a written answer and a few cited sources. A growing practice of generative engine optimization (GEO) monitors which sources and brands these answers show, typically from a single place. In this paper, we present a controlled audit of how the user's location changes the sources that generative engines cite. We ask 300 questions of ChatGPT with 19 declared locations, and of ChatGPT and Gemini from five network locations, each twice to measure run-to-run noise (31,200 answers). The engines take location from different channels. ChatGPT follows the location an application declares, down to the city: it writes the place into its own searches, and its search backend localizes results even when the queries name no place. It ignores the network. Gemini ignores the declared location and follows the country of the network, changing most of its sources even for questions that do not depend on place. The businesses the answers recommend change with the sources. Thus, visibility in generative search is specific to the user's location, and audits must control both channels.

title: LOCU: Lowdin-Orthogonalized Constraint Updates for Multi-Constraint Policy Optimization
summary: We investigate multi-constraint policy optimization in constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs), where interactions among constraint gradients often yield ill-conditioned update directions, causing numerically fragile steps and unintended cancellation or redundant overlap in constraint corrections. To address this, we propose LOCU, which mitigates numerical instability arising from constraint interactions by applying symmetric Lowdin orthogonalization to the natural gradients of the reward and constraints under the Fisher-Rao metric. Combined with Fisher-geometric screening and near-collinear compression, LOCU yields a compact reduced space in which the trust region becomes a Euclidean ball and constraints are handled symmetrically through a low-dimensional active-set solve. For infeasible iterates, LOCU constructs a Pareto-descent direction which preserves the local feasibility of satisfied constraints within the same reduced formulation. Experiments show that LOCU remains stable under high constraint coupling, narrow feasible regions, and infeasible starts, and generalizes across different cost critic architectures.

title: Near-Optimal Last-Iterate Convergence of SGD in the Smooth Interpolation Regime
summary: We study the last iterate of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with a constant stepsize on smooth convex objectives in the low-noise and interpolation regimes, where the variance $σ_\star^2$ of the stochastic gradients at the optimum is small or zero. We establish that after $T$ steps of SGD on $β$-smooth convex losses with any constant stepsize $0<η<2/β$, the last iterate attains expected excess risk $\widetilde O\bigl(\tfrac{1}{η(2-βη)^3T}+\tfracη{(2-βη)^4}σ_\star^2\bigr)$, which gives the rate $\smash{\widetilde O(1/T)}$ for every constant stepsize in the interpolation regime ($σ_\star=0$), matching the $Ω(1/T)$ lower bound up to logarithmic factors and improving upon the $O(1/\sqrt T)$ rate of Attia et al. (2026) for $η=1/β$. Our analysis is based on a new technique, which compares the second moments of the stochastic gradients along the SGD trajectory across only logarithmically many time scales. For quadratic losses in the interpolation regime, an adaptation of this technique gives an $O(1/T)$ rate for every constant stepsize, extending the recent optimal rate for the randomized Kaczmarz method of Derezinski and Dong (2026) to stepsizes above the greedy stepsize with an arguably simpler proof.

title: Cache2LoRA: Understanding and Improving Context Internalization
summary: Context-to-LoRA methods encode documents as low-rank parameter updates, allowing language models to answer without retaining the source text in their decoding context. How reliably do these updates preserve facts and support their use under different instructions? Controlled diagnosis of existing context-to-LoRA methods separates fact discrimination, target retention, and response adaptation. Competing sources influence answers, while target-only construction and memory-state optimization improve recovery at fixed update size. Recovering facts also does not ensure that answers follow response instructions. We introduce Cache2LoRA, which uses each query to aggregate evidence from a reusable frozen document cache before generating LoRA updates. Trainable encoding operates only on the query and memory-token suffix, and multi-style supervision teaches both evidence preservation and answer expression. Across 17 tasks, Cache2LoRA improves on existing context-to-LoRA methods and achieves macro F1 of 0.663, approaching full-context in-context learning at 0.671. For 32K documents and 256-token outputs at batch size 16, its decoding throughput is 5.9$\times$ that of full-context ICL. At matched memory size, generated LoRA preserves answer accuracy more reliably than the learned-KV variant under long, diverse intervening text and combines more effectively with retained document KV, yielding higher hybrid F1 and EM.

title: REFLEX: RNA Ensemble Generation via Flexibility-Calibrated Stochastic Bridge
summary: RNA molecules often function through multiple experimentally observed conformational states. A central challenge is to capture ensemble diversity without sacrificing structural fidelity: samples may collapse toward averaged representative structures or drift into unsupported conformational regions. We introduce REFLEX (RNA Ensemble generation calibrated by FLEXibility), a sequence-conditioned generator for RNA backbone-frame ensembles based on a heteroscedastic stochastic bridge on SE(3). During training, experimental B-factors calibrate residue-wise bridge widths, exposing each observed conformer through local perturbation neighborhoods with residue-specific scales while keeping constrained regions sharper. A learned flexibility condition guides the bridge-field network to recover target conformer-specific frames from these calibrated noisy states. At inference, REFLEX uses only the input sequence, requiring no MSA-subsampling heuristics. On a multi-conformer RNA benchmark, REFLEX achieves the best precision-recall trade-off for ensemble coverage across evaluation thresholds, while recovery-stress ablations indicate gains in target-frame recovery under stronger perturbations.

title: Consistent LLM Call Handling Across Java Frameworks: A Reference Implementation and Benchmark
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables, 1 listing. Code and data: https://github.com/alxkm/llm-call-guard
summary: Java applications reach large language models (LLMs) through an integration framework, and rely on it to handle a failing provider: to retry what can be retried and nothing else, to wait as long as the provider asks, never to present a truncated answer as complete, and to record each failure in the application's metrics. We state these expectations as a six-clause reliability contract and measure Spring AI 2.0.1 and LangChain4j 1.21.0 against it with a scripted OpenAI-compatible provider: fifteen failure scenarios, synchronous and streaming, three repetitions. LangChain4j meets it in 47 of 77 applicable cases with its defaults and in 51 of 83 when configured explicitly, Spring AI in 72 of 77 and 76 of 83; both deliver a stream that ended without its terminator as a complete answer. We then place one implementation of the contract beneath both frameworks, at the HTTP boundary - an OkHttp interceptor for Spring AI, an HttpClient for LangChain4j, and a java.net.http transport for code without a framework - sharing a 725-line core that depends only on the JDK and the Micrometer Observation API. With it, all three clients behave identically and meet the contract in 90 of 91 cases; the remaining case is a policy trade-off between retrying a hung provider and waiting for a slow first token. Against a local model server the layer rejected none of 700 calls, and it adds a median of 32-217 microseconds to a call.

title: Joint, Decoupled, or Agent: When Each Multimodal Alignment Paradigm Wins
summary: Jointly pretrained multimodal encoders are a common way to combine modalities, while alternatives integrate their information during downstream training or inference. When does each approach win? We compare three paradigms, instantiated with public checkpoints, across 16 paired datasets in five domains and multiple training-label budgets. JOINT trains a fusion head on frozen, jointly pretrained encoders. DECOUPLED trains a fusion head on frozen, independently pretrained encoders. AGENT gives a frozen LLM task instructions, labelled examples, available sample text, and supervised unimodal readouts. No paradigm dominates the complete 144 dataset-budget combinations: DECOUPLED wins 54, JOINT 44, and AGENT 46 by mean utility. ScienceQA, MELD, and MetMeme shift from AGENT to fusion as supervision increases. Between the fusion paradigms, JOINT leads on four of five QA datasets across all evaluated budgets, while higher unimodal 5-NN accuracy is associated with a relative shift toward DECOUPLED across eight classification datasets (Spearman $ρ=-0.67$). We test whether representation and task diagnostics predict these preferences on held-out datasets before fitting their candidate systems. A two-step cascade combines these diagnostics with task and budget metadata to select AGENT or fusion, then JOINT or DECOUPLED. Under leave-one-group-out evaluation, it selects the winner in 71.4% of cells versus 54.2% for metadata-only routing, with mean relative regret 0.028 versus 0.057. Using geometry, supervised representation diagnostics, and text-label matching together yields higher accuracy and lower regret than using any one of these sources with metadata. These results connect paradigm preferences to supervision budget, task format, and unimodal 5-NN accuracy. Target-task diagnostics thus support selecting among the three paradigms before candidate fitting.

title: The Scheduler Is a Hidden Retriever: How Asynchrony Shapes Evidence Acquisition in Search Agents
summary: Language-model agents increasingly solve complex tasks through parallel reasoning and asynchronous information gathering. Controlled replay across two model families and three benchmarks shows that delivery timing redirects search decisions made before all results arrive, despite identical initial evidence. Acquisition disagreement reaches up to 24 percentage points above same-order repeat variation. This dependence persists after all initial evidence arrives and through a second search, turning temporary differences in what agents have seen into lasting differences in what they acquire. An acquisition-regret bound with a matching construction shows that invariance at a fixed early arrival count can limit the use of evidence already received. We introduce Confluent Evidence Acquisition (CEA), which instead releases local reasoning when each subquestion's evidence is complete and allocates shared search independently of completion order. For a fixed plan and stable conditional response law, we prove joint invariance of decisions, acquisitions, and answers. With question-only plans across three benchmarks, CEA brings acquisition disagreement to within 1.0 percentage point of repeat variation and achieves accuracy comparable to complete-input controls, improving over early commitment by up to 12.6 percentage points. Replacing CEA's fixed allocation with first-ready allocation under contention adds 21.6 percentage points of acquisition disagreement, while local query-target disagreement remains near repeat variation. Timed comparisons show that CEA reaches decisions earlier and responds faster than the same program waiting for all initial evidence.

title: Probabilistic Limit Order Book Forecasting with Conditional Diffusion Models
summary: Modeling limit order book (LOB) dynamics is central to market forecasting and execution-strategy evaluation. While diffusion models achieve strong empirical performance, existing LOB snapshot models typically lack a learned recurrent encoder and formal statistical guarantees. We introduce LOBGrad, a conditional DDPM framework for probabilistic LOB forecasting that combines an autoregressive RNN encoder with a diffusion-based generator. In particular, we establish an excess-risk oracle inequality for the one-step DDPM noise-prediction objective under exponential mixing and regularity assumptions. We further show that, under contractive dynamics, the dependence on the conditioning-window length can be reduced to a dependence on the latent-state dimension. Experiments on BTC/USDT, GOOGL, and META show that LOBGrad improves on its encoder-free diffusion ablation across all reported queue metrics and obtains competitive results against other baselines. It also reproduces the key stylized facts of LOB microstructure, and yields reasonably calibrated queue-based predictive intervals. A stylized downstream task illustrates the potential value of the generated forecasts.

title: Inside the Loop: A Mechanistic Study of Weight-Tied Transformers on Depth-Bound Algorithmic Tasks
summary: Solving algorithmic tasks with many sequential steps typically requires scaling up transformer depth or chain-of-thought length, incurring unfavorable parameter and inference-compute costs, respectively. Looped transformers, which reuse one block of layers across many iterations, are poised to address this, since they scale effective depth without adding parameters or tokens. Yet, it remains unclear what each iteration is actually computing, or whether the loop merely simulates a deeper untied stack. Here, we study directed permutation traversal, in which a model follows $H$ hops from a starting node and reports the node it reaches, so every intermediate hop has a known ground truth. We find that a minimum effective depth is necessary to solve the task, beyond which the degree of weight tying becomes the determining factor. For instance, a looped transformer with a four-layer block iterated eight times solves the task in every seed, while an identically-trained untied transformer of the same effective depth never does, succeeding only with a lower learning rate or supervision of its intermediate layers. Probing and intervening on the residual stream, we find that the looped model advances through the intermediate nodes gradually, forming a staircase that adapts to its iteration budget, whereas the untied model, at that lower rate, exposes them only in its final layers. Taken together, our results recast looped transformers as iterative program learners, which allocate their iterations to successive steps of the algorithm and solve tasks that identically-trained untied models of the same effective depth do not. Code is available at https://github.com/magnus-sesodia/insidetheloop.

title: Selective Transfer through Sequence Distillation: From Benchmark Knowledge to Backdoor Behaviour
summary: Knowledge distillation is widely used to transfer capabilities from teacher models to student models, but recent work shows that it can also transfer unintended teacher properties. We study whether different hidden teacher properties survive the same distillation channels. Specifically, we compare two properties: benchmark-associated knowledge and refusal backdoors, and show that distillation treats them very differently. Teachers fine-tuned on benchmark data successfully pass that knowledge to students through all four distillation channels we test, including when students are trained only on teacher-generated number sequences containing no natural language or domain content whatsoever. Refusal backdoors tell the opposite story: backdoored teachers achieve near-perfect triggered refusal, yet sequence-distilled students inherit essentially none of this behaviour. Logit-based distillation transfers it substantially, reaching up to 85.5\% triggered refusal in students that saw zero backdoor examples. Distillation is therefore selective, and the selection criterion is not what data the student sees, but what structure the teacher's property has. The code is available at https://github.com/MJonibek/kd-leakage.

title: Steered Not Stirred: Effective Reward Tilting using Surrogate Reward Mixing
summary: Continuous-time generative models, from diffusion models, flow matching, and now flow maps, owe their practical value to high-fidelity generation and steerability. In many applications, a ground-truth latent ``oracle'' reward $R^*$ is unavailable or expensive to evaluate, e.g., human judgments or experimental measurements. Although the oracle reward is not directly observable, it can often be approximated through multiple cheaper surrogates that, individually, provide incomplete characterizations but collectively reveal substantial information about the downstream task. In this paper, we present a method for composing such surrogates to steer a pretrained model toward the distribution tilted by an unavailable $R^*$. Given a small feedback set of oracle rankings or numerical rewards, we introduce Mixing And Reward Tilting for INference-time Improvement (MARTINI), which learns a surrogate composition for plug-and-play use with standard inference-time steering methods. Our theory characterizes surrogate information limits and relates population recovery error to ideal-target KL at small tilt strength. For preferences, the bound additionally accounts for an irreducible mismatch between the Plackett-Luce population target and the conditional mean. Experiments demonstrate improved oracle-tilt fidelity in language generation and ImageNet alignment, and improved joint pose accuracy and validity in protein-ligand cofolding, without inference-time oracle queries.

title: Continual Test-Time Learning with Evolution Strategies
summary: Large language models increasingly operate in open-ended environments, where they are expected to continually adapt to evolving tasks and distributions, often without access to external supervision. Existing continual learning approaches rely on external supervision, such as labeled data, demonstrations, or reward signals, which can be costly or unavailable in practice. Test-time adaptation removes this dependence by learning from self-generated supervision, but existing methods derive that supervision from the single policy being updated, so once the policy drifts, its own learning signal drifts with it, leading to policy collapse, degraded reasoning, and catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we propose \textbf{Evolution Strategy Reinforcement Learning (ESRL)}, a continual test-time learning framework that draws its self-generated supervision from a population of policies instead of the single policy being trained. ESRL perturbs an anchor policy in parameter space to form a population of nearby policies, samples one trajectory from each, and aggregates their answers into label-free group-relative learning signals for the central student. The anchor is held fixed within each block and refreshed from the student at block boundaries, so the population stays centered on a stable yet current policy and continues to supply diverse and reliable supervision as the student moves. In single-task test-time adaptation across mathematical reasoning, general knowledge, and medical domains, ESRL improves average accuracy by up to 31.7% relative to the base model and 16.6% relative to the strongest test-time adaptation baseline. Notably, ESRL substantially reduces catastrophic forgetting and achieves the strongest final performance in continual learning.

title: StrucChunk: Structure-Aware Retrieval for Legal Document RAG
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can ground LLM outputs in domain-specific knowledge, but legal documents are hard: standard chunking fragments hierarchical argument structure, and generic embeddings struggle with both precise citation matching and semantic understanding. We propose StrucChunk (Structure Aware Chunking) with hybrid dense-sparse retrieval for hierarchically structured legal documents. It treats documents as directed acyclic graphs of provisions, preserves clause boundaries, resolves cross-references before embedding, and combines BM25 with BGE-M3 via Reciprocal Rank Fusion. We evaluate on five corpora, three legal traditions and two languages. StrucChunk reaches 100% boundary precision (vs. 7.7% for recursive splitting on CrPC), preserves 97.6% of documented cross-references (vs. 0%), and matches section coverage with 40.3% fewer chunks on GDPR. On LegalBench-RAG (6,858 query-passage pairs), it achieves Char-Recall@8 of 48.18% vs. 23.59% for the best baseline (+104%), surpassing the published state of the art by +83%. On 501 queries each for CrPC and CPC (Indian law), Recall@5 improves from 0.557 to 0.804 (+44.4%) and from 0.158 to 0.259 (+64.6%); chunking accounts for 88% and 73% of the gain. On 501 GDPR queries, Recall@5 is 0.868 with R@1 improving +59%. On NitiBench-CCL (3,730 Thai financial law queries), HR@5 is 0.856 vs. 0.594 for naive chunking (+44.1%), showing that section-boundary alignment is the dominant factor across languages, and cross-reference augmentation adds +2.3% on cross-reference queries. We release the implementation, 5,256 evaluation queries across five legal corpora, annotation methodology and chunking quality metrics. Code: github.com/SinghSuryaDeep/legal-rag-strucchunk-1

title: KPI-Aware Multimodal Anomaly Detection for 5G and Open RAN Telemetry
comment: Accepted at the IEEE ICDM 2026 Applied Research Track
summary: Reliable anomaly detection is a deployment bottleneck for 5G/Open RAN observability and emerging self-optimizing 6G systems, where hundreds of heterogeneous KPIs, severe class imbalance, and strict alert budgets make purely numerical scores brittle. We present KAC, a deployment-oriented KPI-aware multimodal anomaly-detection framework that uses KPI-level residual-text alignment to turn compact operator-style summaries into a learnable feedback signal over full-KPI temporal evidence. This gives the detector broad numerical coverage like modern time-series models, while retaining the sparse KPI-specific reasoning that makes operator feedback sustainable in a future operator-facing workflow. Across public telecom telemetry, enterprise-scale Open RAN observability data, and a Nokia benchmark built from real 5G RAN production packet traces with realism-hardened injected anomalies, KAC achieves strong threshold-based detection performance while remaining competitive on threshold-free ranking metrics. On TelecomTS, at a fixed 2.5 percent false-positive-rate operating point, KAC achieves the highest recall among the evaluated residual-based methods while maintaining comparable precision; across the evaluated benchmarks, it remains robust under substantial class imbalance. KAC is integrated in pre-production shadow mode with Nokia's GKE-based KPI construction pipeline, where it continuously scores telemetry windows alongside an internal packet-level anomaly detector for operational evaluation.

title: Probing Ambiguity: Adversarial Intent Resolution for Robust Text-to-SQL
summary: Text-to-SQL systems typically assume a one-to-one mapping between natural-language queries and correct SQL translations. In practice, however, many queries are inherently ambiguous, admitting multiple valid interpretations that yield distinct outputs. We introduce Adversarial Intent Resolution (AIR), a multi-agent framework that actively probes and resolves such ambiguity without any task-specific training. AIR first constructs competing interpretations, verifies through SQL execution that they produce genuinely different results, and generates targeted clarification questions grounded in the observed data differences. Evaluating on leading benchmarks for ambiguous questions, AIR demonstrates strong performance, efficiency, and robust cross-benchmark transferability. On the AMBROSIA benchmark under schema-only context, a realistic production setting where exposing the full database is infeasible, AIR outperforms IntentRL, the state-of-the-art reinforcement learning model, across all metrics (e.g., F1 0.679 vs. 0.618). Crucially, AIR exhibits only ~7% performance degradation without the full database, compared to ~20% for IntentRL. On the AmbiQT benchmark, where ambiguity arises from schema design rather than linguistic structure, AIR achieves higher F1 under both context settings without any benchmark-specific adaptation.

title: The Control Layer Behind Rule-Following Agents Trading Across Market Conditions
comment: 47 pages, 0 figures, 16 numbered tables. Includes a trading-agent evaluation toolkit and checklist
summary: Trading discipline often fails people. Our study tested whether four AI trading agents followed their strategies and risk rules. Offering traders the evidence and an agent evaluation toolkit to separate luck from following the rules, before giving agents meaningful autonomy or capital. Our study analysed 2,627 closed positions from 12 February to 27 August 2026 across the same asset universe and execution conditions. Most positions were simulated against live prices with a 0.09% round-trip fee; 18% involved real Hyperliquid orders. Each position declared a strategy, stop and target, with a limit of five open positions per agent. The fleet finished net positive after fees. Rule adherence was high across all four agents, including the unprofitable one. Profitability tracked how often agents won relative to their break-even win rates. Institutional-style controls ran by default and contained losses through a 29% market drawdown and recovery, with documented exceptions. The discipline held for all four agents. Agents kept 97.5% of gross loss within declared stops, and typical losses closed at declared levels. Declared risk remained stable after losses and broadly stable across calm and volatile months. Twenty-three of 24 runs respected the position limit; logs identify the exception's size and duration. The same live data produced different results across assigned strategies. The trade-log tests can be rerun from the published trade snapshot; regime tests also require the published Bitcoin prices and regime labels. Section 3.5 specifies the stop-breach tolerance. These trade-level results are not account-level returns or proof of a lasting edge. Our study provides an evaluation toolkit to help traders distinguish rule-following from luck before committing capital. For anyone considering allocating capital to agents to trade, discipline should be the entry test, not the only test.

title: Dynamics-Aligned Representation Learning under Induced Partial Observability
summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has enabled sample-efficient learning of continuous control policies from high-dimensional observations through learned latent dynamics models. These models are typically trained with observation reconstruction objectives, which provide strong supervision but can bias representations toward visual fidelity leading to an undertrained prior and unreliable long-horizon predictions. We propose a stochastic gating mechanism that induces controlled partial observability during training by sampling a spatial binary mask from a Beta--Bernoulli random field and applying it to the raw observation. The gate probability is resampled at each time step, exposing the encoder to conditions ranging from near-total occlusion to near-full visibility. Integration of our method requires minimal architectural changes from existing dynamics models: the gated observation and the binary mask are channel-wise concatenated and passed to the encoder as a single augmented input, with no modifications to the broader training pipeline. We evaluate the proposed approach on a set of pixel-based continuous control tasks selected from the DeepMind Control Suite. Using model predictive control for evaluation, which relies solely on open-loop model rollouts, we show that stochastic gating improves planning performance and data efficiency across tasks. Further analysis demonstrates that performance is robust to the spatial scale of the mask, and a balanced observability during training outperforms configurations biased toward either sparser or denser observations.

title: Not Every User Says It All: Training Tool-Using Agents Beyond Ideal Simulated Users
summary: Tool-using agents are trained and evaluated almost exclusively with strong simulated users who state every detail clearly, yet real users are often weaker. We construct weak users by masking sentences of a simulated user's replies, holding the task and the user's knowledge fixed, and cross-evaluate agents trained with strong and weak users on tau2-bench and ToolWOZ. Weak users lower the success of every policy, and training with them does not help: no policy trained with weak users, through fixed masks, mixtures or a curriculum, serves weak users better than the strong-trained policy beyond run-to-run noise, and prompting the agent to ask more does not help either. We propose StaGPO (State-Grouped Policy Optimization): the agent writes what the task needs, what is missing and how it is being filled, and GRPO uses this state to compare turns of different rollouts that reach the same situation, assigning step-level credit. Within the standard recipe of a small SFT cold start followed by RL, StaGPO makes weak-user training useful: on ToolWOZ, the Qwen3.5-2B policy trained with weak users reaches 76.8% with weak users, the highest of any Qwen3.5-2B policy we trained, 4.8 points above GRPO and 2.8 above the strongest baseline; it is also 5.4 points above GRPO with strong users, and generalises to an unseen mask rate; trained with strong users instead, it serves weak users at least as well as GRPO trained with weak users. On tau2-bench it scores highest with weak users for both models, by a small margin for Qwen3.5-4B.

title: A Generic On-Board AI Processing Chain for Earth Observation: From Application Development to Embedded Deployment and Mission-Level Orchestration
summary: Earth observation satellites acquire more data than they can downlink. Extracting information on board with artificial intelligence (AI) turns the satellite into a data-reduction stage that downlinks compact products, such as masks or detections, instead of full scenes; deploying it in a mission, however, involves the whole processing chain and not only the neural network. We present a generic on-board AI processing chain along three axes, with wildfire segmentation as the worked example among ship detection and cloud segmentation. (i) The AI model is tuned (spectral-band selection, input normalization), quantized to 8-bit integers (int8) and ported to an AMD Versal VCK190, with its excellent segmentation performance preserved on the board. (ii) A modular tiler-inference-mosaicer workflow, reused unchanged across applications, brings the tile-level model to scene level, turning a full acquisition into a scene-level mask or detection list. (iii) Each step is packaged as a unikernel and orchestrated on board by ORCHIDE, a cloud-native orchestrator. The chain is characterized end to end, from the standalone execution on the target to its execution under orchestration with parallel workflows on a representative test bench. Beyond AI inference on individual tiles, this approach aims at increasing the maturity of on-board AI deployment by addressing a complete processing chain, from the acquired scene to the mission-level execution.

title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference
summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.

title: The Judge Can Debias Itself: Awareness and Self-Debiasing for Reliable LLM-as-a-Judge
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge systems are increasingly employed for automated evaluation, yet remain susceptible to systematic biases that undermine their reliability. We demonstrate that the judge can effectively debias itself without additional training. We propose two lightweight strategies: bias-aware prompting, which explicitly alerts the judge to potential target biases prior to evaluation, and self-debiasing, in which the judge critiques the initial judgment for bias influence. To broaden the evaluation scope, we introduce three novel benchmarks--authority bias (fabricated citations), confidence bias (assertive phrasing), and formatting bias (structured presentation)--and evaluate across seven bias types in total. Across three frontier models, self-debiasing improves performance in 20 out of 21 model-bias combinations with gains up to 15 percentage points, while bias-aware prompting also yields consistent improvements. The recent fine-tuned external critic, however, does not generalize as reliably to the newly-introduced bias types (degradation observed in 5 out of 9 cases). Our findings demonstrate that prompting a judge to reason about bias, either preemptively or retrospectively, is a robust and generalizable approach for enhancing evaluation integrity.

title: VibeTraining-Bench: Data-Trainer-Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires agents to diagnose system bottlenecks and coordinate improvements across training and inference. We refer to the agents' capability to jointly optimize training data, the trainer, and the inference harness as cross-component co-design. We introduce VibeTraining-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this capability across tasks spanning terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning. Within each task, research agents start from an identical initial agent system under a fixed resource budget. Guided by validation feedback, they iteratively refine data, trainers, and inference harnesses, then select and submit a final agent system for evaluation on the test set. To prevent reward hacking, we enforce three safeguards: test data isolation, separate research and grading containers, and network restrictions for research agents. Our evaluation results show that frontier research agents substantially improve target agent systems. For example, on SWE-bench Verified, GPT-6-Astra raises the target agent system's performance from 32.9% to 53.7%, comparable to the human-developed instruct model's 55.4%. However, there is still room to improve their ability to co-design and iteratively refine data, trainer, and harness to achieve cumulative performance gains. We hope that VibeTraining-Bench will serve as a unified platform for advancing RSI, deepening our understanding of cross-component optimization for agent systems. Code and data are available at https://github.com/D2I-ai/VibeTrainingBench.

title: FracTS: Hierarchical and Autoregressive Time Series Generation
summary: Time series are ubiquitous across different domains, and the growing use of synthetic data for privacy-preserving sharing, data augmentation, and stress testing makes time series generation increasingly important. Early generative approaches are predominantly autoregressive, which can suffer from low sample diversity, error accumulation, and difficulty modeling long-range dependencies. In this paper, we introduce FracTS, a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine autoregressive model for multivariate time series generation. Inspired by fractal generative modeling developed for images, FracTS adapts the paradigm from 2D to 1D sequences by learning a multi-scale representation that captures global trajectory structure at coarse scales and local dynamics at fine scales while following the autoregressive nature of time series. In contrast to unstructured images, time series are structured, allowing easy automated or designated temporal feature processing optimized for the model, and global (static) feature extraction describing the instances that generate the corresponding time series in the collection. We incorporate them in the generation process to further improve the generation quality. The design naturally handles multivariate dependencies and improves long-horizon temporal coherence without requiring fixed-length inputs. Experiments on five datasets (two conditional, three unconditional) conducted against seven baselines show that FracTS consistently outperforms baselines across marginal distribution and predictive ML utility, and correlation preservation in the unconditional setting. In particular, the predictive ML utility is averagely improved by 100.0% and 75.0-81.0% for unconditional and conditional time series datasets compared to the best baseline (relative error computed on dataset-averaged raw values). Code is available at: https://github.com/BetterdataLabs/fracts.

title: Pluralistic Alignment in Language Models: Objectives, Human References, and Preference Representations
summary: Pluralistic alignment aims to represent meaningful variation in human preferences rather than collapse heterogeneous judgments into a single target. Yet existing work often mixes three distinct questions: what pluralistic behavior a model should exhibit, whose preferences define the reference, and what evidence is sufficient to demonstrate success. We organize the literature around a two-layer taxonomy. Layer 1 distinguishes representing a range of human-supported viewpoints (Overton Pluralism), adapting faithfully to a specified perspective or preference condition (Steerable Pluralism), and matching the response distribution observed in a target population (Distributional Pluralism). Layer 2 distinguishes aggregate populations, countries and regions, and subgroups as human references. Preference representation, implementation mechanism, modality, and evidence quality are treated as cross-cutting design choices rather than additional forms of pluralism. We synthesize a protocol-bounded corpus of 70 works on pluralistic alignment and neighboring areas, using the objective-by-human-reference matrix to map existing approaches and identify underexplored combinations. The coded literature concentrates on Steerable Pluralism and Distributional Pluralism, while eligible Overton Pluralism work appears only at the aggregate-population level under our stated protocol. We then connect each objective to the evidence needed to support it, including perspective validity, conditional fidelity, distributional fidelity, support preservation, and uncertainty in subgroup estimates. Together, the taxonomy and evaluation framework clarify what current methods establish, where their claims exceed their evidence, and how future systems can represent disagreement without mistaking variation for faithful representation.

title: CARRS: A Constraint-Aware, Real-Time Routing System for Emergency Vehicles in Urban Environments
summary: Emergency vehicles such as police vehicles, fire engines, and ambulances require a stable and efficient route optimization to reach life-critical events in the shortest times possible. However, the dynamic nature of urban traffic makes this ideal scenario much more challenging, causing critical life-threatening delays. Traditional civilian navigation systems cannot account for real-time traffic changes alongside vehicle-specific constraints, creating inadequate routing scenarios. This research presents the Constraint-Aware Real-Time Routing System (CARRS), a unified software architecture tailored for emergency coordination. The CARRS architecture is engineered to fuse together classical pathfinding algorithms such as A*, Dijkstra, and Bidirectional A*, with Constraint Satisfaction Problem methodologies. The Design Science Research Methodology is the research framework, and prototyping is the iterative process. The artifact was empirically evaluated using OpenStreetMap data for major metropolitan road networks, combined with simulated dynamic traffic scenarios. Performance metrics focused on route optimality, constraint adherence, rerouting responsiveness, and the potential for future system scalability. Findings revealed the system's capability to generate optimal routes for operationally relevant subgraphs in under 35 seconds, with incremental rerouting responsiveness below 20 seconds. Furthermore, the system achieved more than 90% adherence to vehicle-specific constraints, making the CARRS architecture viable for real-time dynamic routing requirements. This study delivers a routing platform that bridges artificial intelligence-driven optimization with software engineering operational compliance, presenting a practical transformative step toward adaptive emergency vehicle coordination in dynamic urban environments.

title: Reinforcement learning on the EPRI AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment benchmark: diagnosing over-commitment and guiding MILP with learned policies
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly proposed as a fast solver for unit commitment (UC), but standalone agents remain far more expensive than mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). In the first study of RL on the 51-generator, 72-hour benchmark of the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment competition, we trace this gap to the agents' own exploration, close most of it, and show that the resulting policy can accelerate an exact solver. In every configuration tested, Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) and an action-branching Deep Q-Network (DQN) trained from scratch committed about twice the units of a thermal-only MILP optimum, at 39-64% higher cost, whereas a merit-order rule came within 1.6-7% (10-24% when unserved energy is priced). When each unit's decision is sampled independently, spare units insure against random de-commitments. Consistent with this, injecting exploration noise during fine-tuning enlarged a lean policy's fleet, a reward without shaping terms did not remove the over-commitment, and under their training noise the agents outperformed the rule subjected to comparable noise. Imitating the MILP solutions and fine-tuning conservatively brought PPO within 2.6% of the optimum, and these policies had the lowest penalised cost of any evaluated (about 5%). Fixing the fine-tuned policy's confident decisions made the MILP 3.8-8.5 times faster within 0.10-0.25% of the best solution, with a smaller worst case than an imitation-only policy fixing as many variables (1.1% against 8.9%). Because dispatch method and benchmark scope alone shift the reported optimality ratio by up to 3.6% and 9%, we propose a reporting protocol.

title: ProbePO: Sparse Probes, Redistributed Credit for Critic-Free LLM Reinforcement Learning
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Transitioning from Pre-Training to Post-Training
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards assigns one terminal reward to an entire reasoning trajectory, obscuring how individual reasoning steps contributed to the outcome. GRPO broadcasts a group-normalized advantage to every response token, while finer-grained approaches often rely on dense auxiliary rollouts or branching schemes that can also alter the data used for policy updates. We cast the missing middle as budgeted measurement: with a limited rollout budget, which partial solutions should be evaluated, and how should their value estimates refine credit? ProbePO selects partial-solution states with a reward-free uncertainty score and estimates their expected verifier rewards under a capped continuation budget. ProbePO redistributes, rather than replaces, GRPO's trajectory-level advantage across tokens while preserving each trajectory's mean token-level advantage; probe continuations serve only as measurements. Across three DeepSeekMath and Qwen-family models spanning 1.5B-7B parameters, ProbePO consistently outperforms GRPO and achieves the highest accuracy among the four evaluated methods in 16 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. Against dense-probing VinePPO on DeepSeekMath-7B, ProbePO achieves higher accuracy on all six benchmarks with 76% less end-to-end training time.

title: GAIDA: Generative AI for Human-in-the-Loop Document Annotation
summary: Document annotation is a fundamental yet labor-intensive step in building document information extraction systems. While Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Large Language Models (LLMs) can automate parts of this process, we argue that annotation systems should be judged not by how completely they remove human effort, but by how effectively they redirect it toward review and correction. We propose a modular human-in-the-loop architecture that integrates OCR-based extraction, LLM-based semantic pre-annotation, and human validation in a single editable workflow, and present \textbf{GAIDA}, a research prototype serving as its reference implementation. GAIDA supports interchangeable OCR engines, LLM backends, and prompt configurations, and enables stage-specific measurement of annotation effort. In an initial single-annotator, stage-specific study on the FUNSD scanned-form and WildReceipt retail-receipt benchmarks, OCR assistance reduced region-creation and transcription time by up to \textbf{80.9\%}, and reviewing LLM pre-annotations reduced semantic-labeling time by up to \textbf{73.7\%}, despite imperfect pre-annotations of 78.86\% and 86.98\% Micro F1 on FUNSD and WildReceipt, respectively. Finally, we reuse the same implementation, adapting only OCR and prompt configuration, to build and openly release \textbf{AraReceipt}, a manually annotated dataset of 100 Arabic receipt images labeled with 25 key-information classes. The results indicate that imperfect automated outputs provide practical value when presented as editable suggestions under human control.

title: Beyond the record: evaluating probabilistic AI weather forecasts deep in the tail
summary: Can probabilistic artificial intelligence (AI) weather forecasts retain skill beyond their training domain? We compare four state-of-the-art AI models (ArchesWeatherGen, U-Cast, WeatherNext2 and GenCast-mini) with the physics-based IFS-ENS over land in 2022, at 1.5° resolution and lead times of 2--10 days. Monthly ERA5 records from 1979--2021 define common historical boundaries, and we characterize new records set in 2022 by their depth, i.e., the exceedance margin relative to local historical variability. Two proper scores, record-threshold weighted CRPS and Brier score, assess the magnitude and probability of record exceedances across all eligible cases, retaining both missed extremes and false alarms. Verified against ERA5, AI models outperform IFS-ENS for heat and cold records at almost every lead and depth. For heat, the advantage strengthens with depth, partly because IFS-ENS over-forecasts deep records, and largely persists for deeper records under HRES-fc0 verification. For wind, gains erode for deeper records and longer leads. Better tail scores can nevertheless coexist with aggregate probability deficits or surpluses, and some improvements arise chiefly on non-exceedances. Increasing underprediction on progressively more extreme observed subsets can also arise through outcome selection, even for an ideal conditional-mean forecast. These findings establish that native probabilistic AI ensembles retain, and for heat increase, their advantage over IFS-ENS as thresholds move beyond local records, although all advantages narrow with lead time. They caution against generalizing the extrapolation failure reported for deterministic AI forecasts to probabilistic systems, and motivate common verification conventions that separate comparative tail skill, performance on realized extremes, and probabilistic calibration.

title: Axiomatic World Modeling for Physics Reasoning
summary: Recent research-level physics-reasoning benchmarks for LLMs reveal a failure mode that lies not in knowledge or execution, but in modeling the world being reasoned about. Models often silently alter given quantities, fabricate laws, or inject unstated assumptions to force a problem into familiar patterns, and then reason inside this corrupted world. We define this premise-level divergence as modeling drift: the gap between a model's internal axiomatic world model (AWM) and the true physical world specified in the problem. Although RLVR and PRM have yielded substantial gains in mathematics and code, their reward shapes do not directly supervise world modeling in axiomatic domains such as physics. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Axiomatic World Modeling (RLAWM), which optimizes the policy by penalizing divergence between its inferred axiomatic world model and the true physics world. RLAWM probes physics reasoning at two hierarchical levels (modeling and solving), each scored by a physically grounded reward. The modeling reward targets abstract knowledge formulation, evaluating whether the model captures the true axiomatic world before attempting calculation. The solving reward targets instantiated knowledge reasoning, checking whether the model's concrete derivation remains consistent with the axiomatic world. This two-level structure separates what world the model believes it is reasoning in from how it reasons within that world. The framework operates exclusively during training, with no extra cost during inference. RLAWM improves performance by up to +12.2 points on PhysReason and +5.2 on PHYSICS over the baseline. It also generalizes zero-shot across difficulty, source, and domain, with a 2.45x gain and +10 points over the strongest baseline on olympiad-level physics and math.

title: Autonomous intelligence for mining productivity: a multi-agent AI approach to operational value creation
summary: Integrated Remote Operation Centres (IROCs) are emerging as the architectural frontier of Industry 4.0 for capital-intensive sectors such as mining, oil and gas, and energy. Yet two intertwined gaps constrain their evolution towards full autonomy. First, no integrated agentic architecture has been proposed for mining IROCs that orchestrates Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition systems, digital twins, predictive analytics and human-machine interfaces under safety-critical constraints. Second, no evaluation framework jointly addresses the real-time, Health-Safety-Environment, regulatory-auditability and cost-per-decision requirements that govern industrial agentic deployments. This paper makes four contributions. It synthesises industry needs and quantified gains documented in analogous industries that motivate an agentic approach to mining IROCs. It introduces EI2ROC, a three-tier multi-agent architecture combining a Large Language Model orchestrator with specialised monitoring and production-capacityprediction agents communicating through a Model Context Protocol-style tool interface. It provides a critical review of agentic evaluation along six orthogonal dimensions and identifies the industrial blind spot of current benchmarks. Finally, it proposes a multi-dimensional benchmarking framework for industrial agentic AI comprising scenario library, harness, metrics and humancalibration protocol. The paper states explicitly which components are implemented in the current prototype, which belong to the proposed reference design and which remain future work, and reports preliminary cost and latency observations from an operating site. Together, EI2ROC and the benchmarking framework constitute a methodological blueprint transferable across CAPEX intensive industries.

title: FTFM: Factorized Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are becoming a powerful alternative to conventional tabular learning, adapting to new datasets in context without task-specific training. Current architectures, however, face a trade-off: models that preserve cell-level representations are expensive because they repeatedly attend across rows and columns, while faster models collapse each row into a fixed embedding and lose this fine-grained state. We introduce Factorized Tabular Foundation Models (FTFM), which preserve cell representations while factorizing their computation through one contextual latent per row and one per column. Cells no longer attend to one another directly; instead, each cell is updated through the interaction of its row and column latents, reducing repeated attention while retaining feature-specific information. FTFM achieves competitive predictive performance in tabular classification on major benchmarks such as TabArena and BeyondArena.

title: Verifying Human-Written Reasoning References
summary: Evaluating the reasoning of AI systems often relies on human-written reasoning chains as references, yet the logical support for their individual steps is rarely verified. Although prior neuro-symbolic approaches have formalized and checked reasoning, their reported evaluations do not systematically assess whether step conclusions in human-written reference derivations are entailed by their cited premise sets or investigate the sources of failures in those references. To address these limitations, we present a novel reference-centred assessment method for human-written derivations that combines entailment checking against cited premise sets, full-premise rechecking, and failure attribution to examine the reliability of these derivations and their formal representations. We evaluate it on P-FOLIO, using a large language model (LLM) to translate step conclusions into first-order logic (FOL) and the Z3 SMT solver to check entailment. Of 386 derivations examined, 202 (52.3%) meet all our checking criteria, meaning that every translated step is entailed by its stated support and the required target is established under the available FOL representations. Among 230 steps not entailed by their stated support, 191 become entailed when checked against the complete original premises, indicating that most initial failures reflect incomplete or mismatched support rather than unsupported claims. Manual analysis of the remaining 39 cases identifies 21 human reasoning errors, 11 FOL translation errors, and 7 dataset annotation errors. A separate manual audit of 50 randomly sampled steps that passed the entailment checks found 46 faithful FOL translations (92%). These findings suggest that disagreement with a human-written reasoning reference may originate in the reference or its formal representation rather than in the AI system being evaluated.

title: BOSS: Token-Budgeted Online Sampling and Selection for LLM Reasoning
summary: Test-time scaling can improve LLM reasoning, but existing approaches typically adapt generation or apply answer selection after a predetermined generation schedule. We study within-instance allocation: under a hard per-instance prompt-plus-completion token cap, when should inference stop, generate another candidate, or spend residual tokens adjudicating candidates already observed? BOSS is a training-free policy for this three-way decision, with worst-case budget checks before every generation and judge call. Its key contribution is online generation-adjudication allocation under one shared token ledger. Across two Llama-3.1 models and four reasoning benchmarks, BOSS attains the highest accuracy in 22 of 24 model-task-budget cells under the common hard cap. At Llama-3.1-8B and B=4k, it reaches 60.5 macro-average accuracy versus 58.6 for Adaptive-Consistency, 59.1 for TALE-EP, and 58.9 for fixed-schedule League. On identical Stage-I candidate pools, randomized A/B judging with repeated voting improves plurality from 58.4 to 60.3, with the full BOSS selector reaching 60.5. Approximately matched-cost controls further characterize how the benefit of adjudication changes with available inference budget. Together, these results establish generation-adjudication allocation as a distinct design axis for reasoning under strict per-instance caps.

title: Benchmark for Structured Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Perovskite Photovoltaics
summary: While retrieval-augmented language models increasingly serve as literature assistants in the physical sciences, existing benchmarks evaluate them primarily on qualitative text overlap or through model-based scoring rather than against verified experimental ground truth. In experimental materials disciplines such as perovskite photovoltaics, however, the most critical inquiries are inherently quantitative and aggregate measurements across dozens or hundreds of papers. Here, we present a quantitative question-answering benchmark where all 755 ground-truth answers are computed directly from 45,441 measured device records (40,889 human-curated records through 2021 and 4,552 records extracted from 2022-2026 literature). Benchmarking six retrieval architectures over 158,274 passages from 25,662 papers using an open 14B model on a single 24 GB GPU, standard passage retrieval tops out at 16-23% accuracy (compared to 1.6-6.5% zero-shot). In contrast, equipping the language model with read-only SQL execution over the structured device table elevates accuracy to 51.5% on historical and 50.8% on prospective literature -- a 33.01.8 percentage-point advantage over hybrid text retrieval. Aggregate queries spanning extrema, distributions, and filtered record counts prove virtually unsolvable via text retrieval alone, demonstrating that systematic table extraction is an operational prerequisite for literature-scale quantitative inquiry.

title: Neuro-Inspired Inhibitory Message Passing for Accurate and Token-Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning
summary: Multi-agent systems promise to solve problems by bringing together information beyond the reach of any individual agent. Retrieval and tool use can distribute this information across agents, making communication essential to collaboration. A central challenge is keeping crucial evidence visible in each agent's context as messages accumulate. Repeated information can crowd out rare, decisive evidence. Models of cortical circuits suggest a principle for addressing this imbalance: inhibition can selectively suppress shared inputs while preserving sensitivity to weaker signals. We adapt this principle into inhibitory message passing, a training-free communication router that cancels redundant evidence separately for each evidence sentence and receiver. Each round, it forwards evidence sentences restated in agents' messages, delivering each at most once to receivers whose own evidence lacks it and excluding the senders' reasoning and answers. Against standard message passing, accuracy in peer groups rose by 39-77 percentage points across three benchmarks, and tokens per run fell by 10-46%. Gains held across seven open models spanning four to thirty-two billion parameters and two commercial models, in groups up to sixty-four agents, and across multi-agent architectures including peer-to-peer, orchestrator-worker, and multilevel hierarchical organizations. These findings support a scalable design pattern for more accurate and token-efficient multi-agent reasoning.

title: Answer Delivery Under a Shared Token Budget: An Audited Study of Stopping and Finalization
summary: An inference budget is useful only when the system delivers an answer within it. We study a fixed-budget policy combining first-valid-box stopping with a charged finalization cue. On 100 fresh, independently audited GSM8K test questions per model, it improves delivered endpoint accuracy over first-box stopping by 8.0 percentage points for Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and 7.0 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. A prelocked repeat on the same questions gives 7.0 and 10.0 points; neither seed shows a gross harm relative to first-box stopping. The point estimates of incremental physical-slot savings are below one percent. A finalization-only ablation separates cue recovery from stopping, and a fixed scalar reader tests extraction as an alternative explanation. The cue is prior art; the contribution is a component and readout analysis with charged injections and verified paths. Results cover two checkpoints, one task, one prompt family, and two fixed seed conditions.

title: Finite Interaction Lens: Structured Precision Sharing for Vision-Language Models
summary: Identifying which visual interventions interact in a vision-language model requires comparing their joint and separate effects. The resulting four-output difference can be small enough for rounding error to obscure it. We introduce the Finite Interaction Lens (FIL), a mixed-precision method for evaluating finite intervention families. At each selected linear projection, FIL decomposes each candidate's input into a native state, two single-intervention components, and a full-dimensional mixed residual. It projects the single-intervention components at higher precision and reuses the same numerical contributions in the joint candidates, while retaining every mixed residual and nonlinear trajectory. We derive a local cancellation identity and a conditional bound on error propagation through a smooth nonlinearity. In one MLP of Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, FIL reduces final interaction MSE by 94.4% on 16 synthetic families and by 99.85% and 99.35% in two separate four-image COCO studies, relative to a control that has the same nominal BF16-product budget and higher-precision single interventions but projects each joint candidate independently. One image accounts for most of the absolute gain in each COCO study. Higher-accuracy multi-product BF16 arithmetic on all candidates gives lower aggregate error at similar total query times. Single-product BF16 already recovers the reference choices in both candidate-selection tasks we tested. On these development inputs, FIL improves interaction fidelity at a fixed nominal precision budget. Its practical value depends on a task that needs the extra fidelity.

title: Medical Fine-Tuning Reshapes, Not Reduces, Patient-Facing AI Risk: A Rubric-Based, LLM-Judge Evaluation Framework
summary: Patient-facing medical question answering with large language models (LLMs) is moving from research demonstrations to production deployments, yet evaluation remains anchored on factual correctness. Factuality is necessary but not sufficient: a response can be factually grounded and still issue a directive that, if acted on, would harm the patient. We introduce a risk-sensitive evaluation framework that scores responses by the presence and severity of six categories of risk-bearing language (treatment directives, contraindications, dosage expressions, urgency-triage cues, high-alert medication mentions, and overconfident assertions), anchored on published clinical harm taxonomies. Severity is classified by a three-judge LLM ensemble. We apply this framework to six 7-9B instruction-tuned models, three general (Mistral-7B, Phi-3.5-mini, Llama-3.1-8B) and three medically adapted (BioMistral-7B, OpenBioLLM-Llama3-8B, Med42-Llama3-8B), on 200 real patient questions from the K-QA benchmark. Two findings emerge. First, ensemble risk-bearing language is statistically independent of factual hallucination rate (pooled Spearman $ρ= -0.065$, $n = 300$, 95% CI $[-0.18, +0.05]$; distance correlation $= 0.10$, independence test $p = 0.24$). Second, medical fine-tuning does not reduce aggregate risk but reshapes it: continued-pretraining adaptations (BioMistral, OpenBioLLM) consistently suppress high-alert medication mentions while amplifying overconfident assertions, whereas clinical instruction-tuning (Med42) suppresses dosing only, without amplifying overconfidence. Per-category Krippendorff $α$ is fair to good for the four linguistically anchored categories (0.53-0.71) and low for the two clinical-judgment-dependent categories (0.19, 0.31), indicating where automatic safety evaluation is and is not yet reliable. We release the rubric, judge prompts, and evaluation code.

title: Local data augmentation for imbalanced binary classification
summary: Facing imbalanced binary classification, we aim at maximizing the recall while limiting the proportion of false detections in the minority class. For doing that, the present work studies the effect of several rebalancing strategies, from the uniform subsampling of the observations from the minority class, to a more involved local data augmentation scheme. To be more specific, we establish that only rebalancing class proportions cannot modify the classification performance, whereas local data augmentation is proved to have an impact on the final results. The local augmentation scheme is introduced by means of a two-step procedure. The first step randomly subsamples anchor points among the training observations. These anchor points are used in the second step, for drawing new augmentation data following an ''augmentation kernel'' to be specified. This enables us to decouple the impact of the anchor points subsampling from the one of drawing augmentation data accounting (or not) for the local geometry of the support. The experiments on synthetic data illustrate the practical performance of several strategies for subsampling anchor points combined with either a Gaussian or a diffusion-based augmentation kernel. Compared to SMOTE-like data augmentation procedures, a better performance is achieved when subsampling in the close neighborhood to the classification boundary combined with a Gaussian augmentation kernel. Furthermore in specific settings where the geometric structure of the support matters, the experimental results show that using a diffusion-based augmentation kernel outperforms the Gaussian one.

title: CVTA: Cross-Variable Temporal Attention for Multivariate Irregular Time Series Prediction
comment: Accepted at the Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Main Track
summary: Irregularly sampled multivariate time series arise in many real-world domains such as healthcare, climate science, and large-scale monitoring systems. Characterized by asynchronous observations and heterogeneity across variables, such time series pose significant challenges for forecasting. In this work, we introduce Cross-Variable Temporal Attention (CVTA), a short-term, continuous-time forecasting framework that learns prediction functions from its compact, interpretable state summarizing recent temporal dynamics across variables. CVTA uses Variable-Conditioned Embeddings to project heterogeneous variables into variable-specific latent spaces, and applies temporal attention to capture cross-variable dependencies from this state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that CVTA can be integrated as an auxiliary module into existing state-of-the-art prediction models through a dynamic meta-decision model. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks show that CVTA achieves strong short-term predictive accuracy, supports efficient online inference, improves existing prediction models when used as an auxiliary module, and learns attention patterns that align well with domain knowledge.

title: Bellman Language Models: Solving the Recurring Decisions of LLM Agents
summary:
A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. LLMs generally don't treat these decisions as an optimization problem and instead re-derive them from their context/prompt on every turn. We show that treating decision making within reasonable bounds as an optimization problem, solving it once, and reusing the solved decisions can often make an agent faster, cheaper and more reliable. Our approach, which we call Discretize, Then Decide, starts from data such as the workflow's own logs or, when none exists, runs of the LLM agent itself. It reads each conversation into discrete states and estimates the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move, until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing. It then solves the resulting Markov decision process. The solution runs as a controller around the model, sending moves whose content is fixed in the state, such as a tool call or a templated reply, and any state it hasn't seen is sent back to the LLM. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman's equation for the best move in each state.
  On $τ^2$-bench telecom, the controller with no model solves 79% of tasks. As a BLM, Qwen3.8-27B, an open model, goes from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls. For Claude Opus 5.5, which solves 96% of tasks on its own, running it as a BLM cuts model calls and cost per task by about 98% and lets it solve 2 more tasks. On InventoryBench, the solved policy with no model beats every published method. Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, such as resolving SymPy issues, few decisions can be solved in advance, and a BLM helps little.

title: Physiology-Aware Graph Attention for Early Ventricular Reentry Prediction
summary: Sudden cardiac death mostly originates from post-infarct ventricular tachycardia. This reentry is sustained by propagation around scar tissue, but its risk remains difficult to predict from infarct imaging alone. While in silico induction studies can reveal these mechanisms, exploring many substrates and pacing locations remains computationally expensive. We propose a graph attention classifier for early prediction of sustained ventricular reentry from simulated cardiac electrophysiology. Each simulation is represented as a graph with early nodal voltage samples and edge attributes encoding geometry, stimulation frequency, tissue labels, amplitude, and diastolic interval. These descriptors are computed only from the first two paced activations, before sustained reentry is observed. On a balanced independent test set of 1000 simulations, the classifier achieves 94.6% accuracy, 95.4% sensitivity, 93.8% specificity, 94.6% F1-score, 0.987 ROC-AUC, and 0.985 PR-AUC. Ablation experiments show that diastolic interval is the most critical descriptor. Qualitative attention inspection suggests that different heads focus on border-zone, stimulation location, and early propagation path. These results support graph attention as a fast early-prediction approach for large-scale in silico ventricular reentry studies.

title: Divergence based Ranked Preference Alignment for LLMs
summary: Alignment of large language models typically relies on pairwise preference feedback, though ranked feedback can capture more comprehensive information across multiple responses within a single annotation. However, ranked-preference alignment is underexplored in practice compared to simpler pairwise approaches, potentially resulting in suboptimal behavior. Concurrently, recent research has conceptualized large language model alignment objectives as divergence estimators between aligned (preferred) and unaligned (less-preferred) response distributions, resulting in a family of objectives with an interpretable theoretical foundation and strong empirical performance. This work unifies these perspectives by introducing $f$-RPO, a $f$-divergence objective for ranked preference optimization that extends divergence-based alignment to ranked feedback and recovers pairwise preference alignment as a special case.
